doc.title: Artie Shaw — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Early years: Cleveland, Aaronson, New York
title: Complaint to the Smithsonian about omitting Jean Goldkette
summary: Shaw says he wrote to the Smithsonian and critics that its Big Band Jazz album ignored Goldkette's band, with Bix and Tram, and got no reply.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him

blocks.x: I was there listening. Of course. I wrote that to the Smithsonian, by the way, on that album they put out, Big Band Jazz, from the beginning. Good God. They start out with Paul Whiteman. I wrote, where was Jean Goldkette? He was the only American jazz band worth talking about in that, in the ’27s. They keep talking about Fletcher [Henderson]. Jean Goldkette had one hell of a band. I said, what about listening . . . why didn’t you guys listen to Clementine? One of the great records of that period.
Yeah, but Clementine, wow. That chorus Bix played.

Tremendous, the first 8 [bars] and last 8. Remarkable. Well, what are you going to say? You have geniuses like Gunther Schuller there, who never played a note of jazz in their lives, and they’re telling us what jazz is about. Pretty sad. He gets in there and talks a lot. I wrote a letter to them, and I had copies to Whitney, copies to every jazz critic in America. No-one acknowledged the letter.
It’s astounding. I said I was dumbfounded, flabbergasted, thunderstruck by what they had done.
No, I think you’re right too.

Who did that? How could you leave out . . . from the beginnings? Good God. I don’t know of a band . . . I travelled to hear Jean Goldkette, and the first time I heard that band—I have it in my book—my kid says, “He stood in front of the band and listened to Bix and Tram. The sound they got out of the horns.” He’s not talking about the notes. The sound. That’s ignored today. People make unpleasant sounds, and they call that jazz. I don’t know what they’re talking about. There’s a certain school of thought today that if it isn’t . . . doesn’t sound like broken crockery, it isn’t jazz. God help you if you play melodically. Good help you if it’s good to the ears.
